title: 48-core headline: Dragonfly 15.5M, realistic Redis cluster 4.6M, driven ceiling 40.6M ops/s
statement: Read-heavy (SET:GET 1:10), 100-byte values, pipeline 16, 48 physical cores: Dragonfly (one process) 15.5M ops/s; Redis Cluster driven by one normal cluster-mode client 4.6M ops/s; the same Redis Cluster fully driven with one load generator per shard 40.6M ops/s. Valkey tracks Redis within a few percent (4.5M / 40.2M). Dragonfly = 3.4x the realistic cluster and 38% of the raw ceiling.
caveat: All three numbers are real and describe different client situations. The 40.6M ceiling needs flawless per-shard routing and a client as large as the server; a normal application sees the realistic number.

title: Dragonfly overtakes a realistic Redis cluster at about 16 cores
statement: Below 16 cores a realistic Redis cluster is ahead (4c: 3.2M vs 2.0M; 8c: 5.0M vs 3.7M). At 16 cores Dragonfly passes it (6.5M vs 5.0M) and keeps climbing to 15.5M at 48 cores while the realistic cluster stays flat around 5M.
caveat: Read-heavy pipelined workload. With 1KB values the crossover moves later and Dragonfly flattens at 4.8M from 24 cores.

title: A single cluster-mode client under-reports a Redis cluster by ~9x
statement: One normal cluster-mode client plateaus at ~5M ops/s regardless of shard count, with shards sitting ~16% idle; one load generator per shard reaches 40.6M on the same cluster. That is why every cluster number is reported two ways: 'cluster' (realistic) and 'cluster-sat' (ceiling).
caveat: This is a client-side routing/queuing limit, not a Redis engine limit. Multi-threaded, per-shard clients can approach the ceiling in production.

title: Latency at 48 cores: Dragonfly and a well-driven cluster are sub-millisecond; a naive cluster client balloons to ~84 ms p50
statement: Read-heavy pipelined, 48 cores: Dragonfly p50 0.883 ms / p99 2.423 ms / p99.9 3.327 ms. Redis cluster ceiling p50 0.559 / p99 1.511 / p99.9 4.639 ms. Redis cluster realistic p50 83.967 / p99 138.239 / p99.9 150.527 ms — client-side queuing, not server time.
caveat: All latencies are memtier client-side. Never compare an engine's INFO latency with another engine's — Dragonfly's INFO includes network and queue time, Redis/Valkey's does not.

title: Memory: Dragonfly 146 bytes/key vs Redis 165 vs Valkey 169 (about 12-13% leaner)
statement: 1M keys x 100-byte values, baseline-subtracted RSS: Dragonfly 146.1 bytes/key, Redis 165.3, Valkey 168.7.
caveat: Garnet and KeyDB were NOT part of the memory measurement; do not quote bytes/key for them. The vendor's '30% better memory efficiency' figure was not reproduced on this workload; 12-13% was.

title: Multi-key commands: Dragonfly runs MGET/MSET across the keyspace; a cluster rejects them (CROSSSLOT)
statement: Dragonfly single process, pipeline 16: MGET(10) 2.4M ops/s and MSET(10) 1.3M ops/s at 48 cores. Redis and Valkey Cluster reject MGET, MSET, MULTI and multi-key Lua unless every key hashes to the same slot (hash tags).
caveat: Operational-simplicity axis, hardware-independent. Hash-tag co-location works around it at the cost of data-model constraints.

title: Pipelining is the single biggest knob: pipeline 16 vs 1 is ~5x on Dragonfly at 48 cores
statement: Read-heavy, 100B, 48 cores: Dragonfly 2.8M ops/s at pipeline 1 vs 15.5M at pipeline 16; realistic Redis cluster 1.4M vs 4.6M. Without pipelining every engine is bound by round trips, not by CPU.
caveat: Report the pipeline depth with every number; vendor headline figures usually use deep pipelines.

title: KeyDB 6.3.4 hit a wall: weak scaling to 16 threads, then refuses to start
statement: Read-heavy pipelined: 413K ops/s at 4 cores, 569K at 8, 636K at 16 (doubling 8 to 16 bought 12%). With server-threads above 16, KeyDB 6.3.4 exits with 'FATAL CONFIG FILE ERROR ... Invalid number of threads specified' — no 24- or 48-core runs exist.
caveat: Session 2, same harness and instance type as session 1. The wall is a configuration hard limit in this version, not a measured plateau at 24/48.
vendorClaim: KeyDB is a multithreaded database and will outperform Redis on a per-node basis.

title: Garnet 2.1.6 reached at least 21.4M ops/s at 48 cores — client-limited, so a floor not a ceiling
statement: Read-heavy pipelined: 4.1M at 4 cores, 8.1M at 8, 15.8M at 16, 19.0M at 24, 21.4M at 48, with sub-millisecond p50 throughout (0.68 ms at 48c). At 48 cores the CLIENT box saturated first, so 21.4M is a floor. At 16 cores Garnet had already passed the 15.5M that Dragonfly posted at 48 cores in session 1.
caveat: Always say 'at least 21.4M, client-limited'. Dragonfly's 15.5M is from session 1; the two sessions used the same instance type but different instances and dates, so label any cross-session comparison as such. Garnet was not part of the memory measurement.
vendorClaim: Garnet exhibits better scalability than Redis or KeyDB

title: Never compare INFO latency across engines; memtier client-side latency is the only common yardstick
statement: Dragonfly's INFO latency counts network and queue time; Redis and Valkey's INFO does not. The benchmark therefore reports memtier client-side p50/p99/p99.9 for every engine and never quotes server-side INFO figures.
caveat: Applies to any vendor page that quotes its own INFO numbers against another engine's.

title: Redis executes commands on one thread, so using 48 cores means a 48-shard cluster
statement: Redis's own docs: 'Redis is, mostly, a single-threaded server from the POV of commands execution ... It is not really fair to compare one single Redis instance to a multi-threaded data store.' The benchmark therefore never pits one Redis process against Dragonfly; it pits a Redis/Valkey Cluster with one shard per core against one Dragonfly process, and reports throughput per node.
caveat: Redis 8 and Valkey 8 have I/O threads, which help network handling, not command execution; the per-core shard count still decides scale.
vendorClaim: Redis is, mostly, a single-threaded server from the POV of commands execution (actually modern versions of Redis use threads for different things). It is not designed to benefit from multiple CPU cores.

title: Valkey 8.1.9 tracks Redis 8.2.8 within a few percent on every axis
statement: Realistic cluster 4.5M vs 4.6M, ceiling 40.2M vs 40.6M, memory 168.7 vs 165.3 bytes/key, latency profiles overlap. Choosing between them is a licensing and ecosystem decision, not a performance one, on this workload.
caveat: Same configuration for both; no Valkey-specific tuning was attempted.
